etymologies.etymologyHTML: From French veste (“a vest, jacket”), from Latin vestis (“a garment, gown, robe, vestment, clothing, vesture”), from Proto-Indo-European *wéstis, from *wes- (“to be dressed”) (English wear). Cognate with Sanskrit वस्त्र (vastra) and Spanish vestir.

definitions.definition: (Canada, US) A sleeveless garment that buttons down the front, worn over a shirt, and often as part of a suit; a waistcoat.

quote.citation: 1913, Joseph C[rosby] Lincoln, chapter X, in Mr. Pratt’s Patients, New York, N.Y., London: D[aniel] Appleton and Company, →OCLC:
quote.text: The Jones man was looking at her hard. Now he reached into the hatch of his vest and fetched out a couple of cigars, everlasting big ones, with gilt bands on them.

definitions.definition: (British) A sleeveless garment, often with a low-cut neck, usually worn under a shirt or blouse.
A sleeveless top, typically with identifying colours or logos, worn by an athlete or member of a sports team.
Any sleeveless outer garment, often for a purpose such as identification, safety, or storage.

quote.citation: 2010, Thomas Mullen, The Many Deaths of the Firefly Brothers, Random House, →ISBN, page 162:
quote.text: He gripped some of the shreds and pulled off his vest and the shirt beneath it, his clothing disintegrating around him. What in the hell point was there in wearing a twenty-five-pound bulletproof vest if you could still get gunned to death?
In state attended by her maiden train, / Who bore the vests that holy rites require.
Not seldom, clad in radiant vest / Deceitfully goes forth the morn.

definitions.definition: (now rare) A loose robe or outer garment worn historically by men in Arab or Middle Eastern countries.
(chiefly passive) To clothe with, or as with, a vestment, or garment; to dress; to robe; to cover, surround, or encompass closely.

quote.citation: 1673, John Milton, Methought I Saw my Late Espoused Saint:
quote.text: Came vested all in white, pure as her mind.
With ether vested, and a purple sky.

definitions.definition: To clothe with authority, power, etc.; to put in possession; to invest; to furnish; to endow; followed by with and the thing conferred.

quote.citation: c. 1718, Matthew Prior, To Mr. Howard - An Ode:
quote.text: Had thy poor breast receiv’d an equal pain; / Had I been vested with the monarch’s power; / Thou must have sigh’d, unlucky youth, in vain; / Nor from my bounty hadst thou found a cure.

definitions.definition: To place or give into the possession or discretion of some person or authority; to commit to another; with in before the possessor.

quote.text: Empire and dominion […]  was vested in him.

definitions.definition: (law) To clothe with possession; also, to give a person an immediate fixed right of present or future enjoyment of.

quote.citation: 1765–1769, William Blackstone, Commentaries on the Laws of England, (please specify |book=I to IV), Oxford, Oxfordshire:  […]  Clarendon Press, →OCLC:
quote.text: For the right of the crown vests […] upon his heir.

definitions.definition: (law, intransitive) (of an inheritance or a trust fund) To devolve upon the person currently entitled when a prior interest has ended.
(financial, intransitive) To become vested, to become permanent.

quote.citation: 2005, Kaye A. Thomas, Consider Your Options, page 104:
quote.text: If you doubt that you'll stick around at the company long enough for your options to vest, you should discount the value for that uncertainty as well.

quote.citation: 2007, Ransey Guy Cole, Jr. (United States Court of Appeals, Sixth Circuit), Roger Miller Music, Inc. v. Sony ATV Publishing, LLC
quote.text: Sony interpreted 17 U.S.C. § 304 as requiring that the author be alive at the start of the copyright renewal term for the author’s prior assignments to vest.
